I'm very new to github, but have a fairly decent understanding of how lake reads json files and such, but I am not very sure at all what to do (or what PATH means exactly in this specific context). If somebody could help me with how to set up Comparator, landrun, and lean4export I would appreciate it.

I've cloned them all into my project root, and would like to run Comparator locally in private first, before figuring out how to get it going for public consumption. I have a github repo but it is currently set to private.

And yes. #print axioms is nice and clean. :)

I have tried for example to run "go build -o landrun cmd/landrun/main.go" from the landrun directory, but I get a red warning in shell that tells me "go : The term 'go' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet, function, script file, or operable program..."
In general that means you need to install golang. That being said your error sounds like a windows error and comparator does only work with linux at the moment.
Oh man. (EDIT: lol I forgot I can just set up a VM)
But I can still set it up on my github repo right? At the very least other people can use it that way, or is that not how it works?
Ok I'll set up a virtual environment or something...
It is in principle possible to set it up on your GH repo yes

But that is not how it is usually done?

My understanding is extremely superficial.. I know you expose your code on a public repo (at least I think I know), and then I see that you can set up a comparator link now so people using the live version of lean can just click it and check the code, but is that supposed to run on your own machine (which really doesn't make sense to me) or aren't you supposed to have it up on a server like github so its always accessible?

You just need that repo and run it, then show the results. The GH way needs to spin up a VM then do the same.

It might help checking what this guy did in his #AI authored projects > Can someone check my proof in universal algebra/clone theory

He got comparator to pass as a GH action. And in terms of how it is usually done, in my experience this is the first time I have seen it as a GH action. Usually people just build it and report the results from what I have seen.

Thanks Yan, yeah that thread is how I found out about it. Then found the thread #general > Comparator Live now available from the Live Lean playground @ 💬 with the install instructions which promptly got me worrying about how much I really understood.

Isn't it kind of defeating the purpose, if you can just run it and later post that you got a good result? Kind of "we trust you but we dont trust but you but ok we trust you.." It looked to me that the whole point of the program was so people could run it themselves on your code.

Yea differing levels of trust I suppose, one is a trusting a person genuinely thinks they proved something, and the other is just trusting they won't blatantly lie.

All that would happen then is someone else will run it and it will fail, and the person who lied would take a real big reputational hit.
I think I am getting this sorted out, AI is fairly helpful.

Is lean4export supposed to be under the exported directory? I am confused that seems backwards.

I have rootfolder/src/(library 1/ and library2/) and i have lean4export in the rootfolder, needing to export from library2/ but a) I cant get that to work and b) I'm not sure if I am supposed to build a new folder underneath the one holding the module I want to export.

Forgot, this was the command I was trying in various configurations:
lake env ~/projects/lean4export/.lake/build/bin/lean4export library2.foo -- final_theorem > lemma.ndjson
No matter what I did, lean kept telling me it couldn't find the module at the path given. Does lean4export maybe only look at the first library?
Here's how I set it up fwiw: https://github.com/brettkoonce/lean4-mlir/blob/main/.github/workflows/comparator.yml

I think my problem is that I don't understand exactly how PATH works in this context. I've got a compiling project with ROOT/src/project_libraries but when I try to use lake env with lean4export, it only searches the .lake/ directory, which is in my ROOT, and completely skips the src/ folder. I tried to figure out what you did Brett, but I think its been a few too many years since I worked with Unix/Linux..

I fixed the PATH issue. I can get the env command to run and return output in the command line beyond essentially "no", but I can see the problem is that I have two libraries and it does only look at the first one. Everything I have tried to do to fix this, makes the project unbuildable. I even tried to change the file structure and put everything under one big umbrella, and edited every single import/export/namespace/end command line to match, and it refused to compile.

EDIT: I think I figured this out, as well.

I did it locally on my machine first before moving to the cloud fwiw. Comparator itself is a just a fancy way of running your lean proofs --> I would focus on the code first. If you have a github repo of your code/are willing to share I could try to build you a config if that helps!

Yeah I am trying to get it to build locally, first. I got lean4export to run on my final proof theorem and I get a huge file out of it, so I think that is working. I've got landrun installed and if I "which landrun" I get "/usr/local/bin/landrun" so I think that is working correctly?

I'm now stuck on comparator itself. I've got it installed I think, but if I try to "lake exe" I dont have any executables. My lakefile for this project is 

import Lake
open Lake DSL

package DiscreteDynamics where
   binRoot := "exe"

require mathlib from git
   "https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4.git" @ "master"

@[default_target]
lean_lib Presentations where
   srcDir := "src"

lean_lib Analysis where
   srcDir := "src"

lean_exe Comparator where
   root := `ComparatorMain

and I built an /exe folder in the root with a ComparatorMain.lean file in it with 

import Comparator
open Comparator

def main : IO Unit := do
   let args ← IO.getArgs
   match args with
   | #[dir] =>
      Comparator.runOnDirectory dir
   | _ =>
      IO.println "Usage: comparator <directory>"

But I'm pretty sure something is wrong there as clearly it doesn't work...

You're importing comparator directly. Here's the pieces/idea:

Challenge.lean --> theorem two_plus_two : 2 + 2 = 4 := by sorry
Solution.lean  --> theorem two_plus_two : 2 + 2 = 4 := rfl
config.json --> {
    "challenge_module": "Challenge",
    "solution_module": "Solution",
    "theorem_names": ["two_plus_two"],
    "permitted_axioms": ["propext", "Quot.sound", "Classical.choice"],
    "enable_nanoda": false
}

lake build Challenge Solution
lake env comparator config.json

Then comparator literally validates that only the three permitted axioms are in the output list.

You shouldn't need lake_exe Comparator, you should clone the comparator repo and lake build in that directory, which will put the comparator binary at a path that looks like /path/to/comparator/repo/.lake/build/bin/comparator

The README for Comparator is confusing on this point because of the need to do a workaround to handle the sandbox escape in Landrun, but if you ignore that complication, it's saying to run, at the command line, 

lake env path/to/comparator/binary path/to/config.json

that's in the directory where your Solution and your Challenge are

When I run Comparator, I do something like this:

PATH=$PATH:$PWD/../lean4export/.lake/build/bin:$PWD/../landrun lake env $PWD/../comparator/.lake/build/bin/comparator path/to/config.json

in order to get landrun and lean4export on my PATH, but there are lots of ways to achieve the same effect

(oops, sorry for clashing with you @Brett Koonce) — yes, if you add comparator as a dependency to your project, you should also just be able to say lake env comparator instead of giving a whole path to comparator
Ahh ok, I think I must have had it set up correctly the first time. Thanks so much, guys!

Ok thanks everybody for the help. I finally got it to run.

Running Lean default kernel on solution.
Lean default kernel accepts the solution
Your solution is okay!

Kevin Buzzard mentions here #AI authored projects > AI-assisted MDS and spectral PRs @ 💬 and I think several other threads as well, that the challenge.lean file should only import Mathlib.

I tried to remove the other imports from my version, and I cannot get the code to compile because comparator/lean no longer knows what the definitions are for the parameters in the thesis statement. I otherwise only have the single theorem proved by : sorry, but I need to import my project (mirroring the imports of the module containing the statement, plus the import of the module containing the statement) or it just doesn't run. I don't know if I set it all up wrong?

Does the export message look right? I don't know what to look for yet.

Put the necessary definitions in the Challenge file with their implementation filled with sorry.
This should allow you to have a Challenge file only depending on Mathlib.
Thanks again, Alfredo!! :D
I don't know why but I had it stuck in my head that you could only have the theorem itself in the file... I think from the README perhaps.

Yes you can put definitions holes, but like it's said in the docs, they can be used to validate a proof by reflexivity.
That's why, any definitions in your solution file still needs to be reviewed by a human.
I thought you said you weren't a mathematician.
I'm not a professional mathematician, but i use lean to prove software right. it's almost the same game just different expertise ;)

Regarding the definitional holes: In that case, isn't it better to have the challenge import the actual code so it can pick up the definitions? It's still got the sorry in it after the by clause so without the solution file it can't cheat that way...

I'm wondering if one could use Comparator to label certain parts of a repository as "merely true". For example, I made a "fast" Lean implementation of discrete convolution (modulo 2) and had an AI write a 8kloc proof that it equals the definition which fits in a single line. This function is used as part of a library which is mostly not AI generated (except some proofs) and where a single challenge file would be too big for a human to review, even if I decided to have such a file. I want to say: "this one folder of 8k lines just proves equality of these two definitions. Assuming you trust the rest of my library, there is no need to look at that folder since it's just ugly proofs. It also can't install malware on your system". While saying all of that is probably impossible, could one come close somehow?

I could make separate repositories, one only containing the large proof, another with the comparator setup (as done in kim-em/erdos-unit-distance-comparator), and import the proof-repository as a package in my main library. But this seems fairly complicated and I guess anyone worried about running AI-generated code they haven't read not trust such a setup?

Maybe I'm looking at a way to "bootstrap" trusted code, as in Metamath Zero? Then again, "just use something like mm0" seems like a tough choice, given one has to forego all the tools and community work going into Lean.

(sorry if this is highjacking the thread. I'm very uncertain in this case if making a new topic would have been better)
